analogy.p: Think of a new drug as a new aeroplane design. Engineers first test models and parts in a workshop and wind tunnel (preclinical tests on cells and animals). Next a test pilot flies it empty or lightly loaded (healthy volunteers at a low dose). Only after it proves safe do real passengers fly (patients), and aviation authorities check all the records (peer review and licensing) before it enters service. This works because safety is proved in small steps before risk is increased. It breaks down because a plane's behaviour is designed and predictable, whereas a drug interacts with living bodies that vary between people.

bullets: **Drug**: a substance that changes how the body works, used to treat, cure or prevent disease or to relieve symptoms.
Traditionally drugs were **extracted from plants and microorganisms**.
Most new drugs are now **synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry**, though the starting point may still be a chemical found in a plant.
Every new drug must be **tested and trialled** before it is used, to check **toxicity, efficacy and dose**.
The testing is in two big phases: **preclinical** (lab, cells, tissues and live animals) then **clinical** (human volunteers and patients).
The whole process takes many years and costs very large amounts of money, which is why a new drug is expensive and why companies patent it.
core.p: AQA 4.3 (Infection and response) expects you to **describe the process of discovery and development of new drugs**. You must know where drugs have traditionally come from, how modern drugs are made, and the stages of testing a new drug must pass (preclinical and clinical) before doctors are allowed to prescribe it. Higher and Foundation tier both need this; it is a favourite 4 or 6 mark extended-response topic because it links biology to ethics and to how scientists check each other's work.

bullets: **Digitalis** is extracted from the **foxglove** plant. It is used as a **heart drug** (it affects heart rate and strength of contraction). Too much is poisonous, which shows why dose matters.
**Aspirin** is developed from **salicylic acid**, a chemical found in **willow bark**. It is a **painkiller**, reduces fever and inflammation, and a low dose is also used to reduce blood clotting.
Early use of willow bark was by chewing or as a tea, but this gave a variable dose and irritated the stomach; chemists later modified the chemical to make a safer, more reliable tablet.
Rainforests and other habitats contain many plants not yet studied, which is one reason **biodiversity** is valuable: unknown species may contain useful drugs.
Link to other topics: plant chemical defences (4.3 plant disease) explain why plants contain such powerful chemicals.
core.p: For thousands of years people used plant extracts as medicines before anybody understood why they worked. Scientists later isolated the **active chemical** from the plant, worked out its structure and tested it. This is why many modern drugs are copies of, or developed from, chemicals found in plants. Plants make these chemicals as defences against pests and diseases, so many of them have strong effects on animal bodies.

bullets: **Penicillin** is an **antibiotic** made by the mould **Penicillium**. It kills bacteria but does not harm human cells and does not work against viruses.
Fleming left a plate of bacteria uncovered; the clear zone around the mould where bacteria had not grown showed that the mould made a chemical that killed bacteria.
Years later Florey and Chain developed methods to extract and purify penicillin and produce it in large amounts, so it could be used to treat patients.
This shows that a discovery on its own is not enough: it needs **development** (purifying, testing, manufacturing) before it can help people.
Link to other topics: antibiotic resistance (bacteria evolve resistance so penicillin no longer works on some strains).
core.p: Microorganisms such as moulds and bacteria also make chemicals that kill or stop the growth of competitors. This was discovered by chance in 1928 when **Alexander Fleming** noticed that bacteria did not grow near a **Penicillium mould** that had contaminated a culture plate. The mould was making a chemical that killed the bacteria.

bullets: Chemists may use a plant chemical as a **starting point** and modify the molecule so it works better or has fewer side effects.
Synthesising the drug gives a **pure, standard dose** each time, unlike a plant extract whose strength varies.
Thousands of candidate chemicals may be made and screened but only a few ever reach patients.
Each candidate must then pass the **same testing stages** whether it came from a plant, a microorganism or was made from scratch.
Drug companies are businesses, so cost, profit, patents and the time before a drug can be sold also affect which drugs are developed.
core.p: Today most new drugs are **synthesised (made artificially) by chemists** working for pharmaceutical companies. They may start with a chemical that occurs naturally in a plant, then change its structure to make it more effective, safer or easier to produce. Making drugs in a factory means large, consistent amounts at a controlled quality, and does not depend on harvesting rare plants.

bullets: **Toxicity**: how harmful the drug is; testing finds out if it is poisonous or causes damaging side effects.
**Efficacy**: how well the drug works, meaning whether it produces the desired effect (treats the disease or relieves symptoms).
**Dose**: how much of the drug to give; testing finds the **optimum dose**, the amount that gives the best effect with the fewest side effects.
Too low a dose is not effective; too high a dose is harmful or toxic. This is the reason for the dose figure in the SVG graph.
Testing also finds **side effects** and how the drug is absorbed, distributed and removed by the body.
core.h: Why new drugs must be tested: toxicity, efficacy, dose
core.p: The specification states that new medical drugs have to be tested and trialled before being used to check that they are safe and that they work. Each key word has an exact meaning you must be able to define, because mark schemes award marks for using them correctly.

bullets: First tested on **cells and tissues** grown in the lab to see whether the drug has the intended effect and is toxic to cells.
Then tested on **live animals**, because a whole body has organs working together and a drug may be affected by digestion, the liver and the kidneys in ways cells in a dish cannot show.
Animal tests check **toxicity**, **efficacy** and the right **dose range** before moving to humans.
Using animals raises **ethical issues**: some people believe it is wrong to cause animals suffering, while others argue it is necessary to protect people.
Many drugs fail at this stage and never reach clinical trials, saving human volunteers from harm.
core.p: Before any human takes a new drug, it is tested in the laboratory. This is called **preclinical testing**. It checks that the drug is not obviously dangerous and that it is likely to work, so people are not put at risk without good reason.

bullets: Trials begin with **healthy volunteers**, using a **very low dose** to check the drug is safe and to look for side effects.
If it is safe, trials continue with **patients who have the illness** to find the **optimum dose** and whether the drug really works (efficacy).
Dose is gradually increased in different groups of patients to find the best balance between benefit and side effects.
Patients may be asked to give **informed consent**: they are told the risks and agree to take part.
Results from all stages must be recorded accurately and shown to be reliable before the drug can be licensed.
core.p: If preclinical results are good, the drug moves to **clinical trials** on humans. Trials go in steps, starting cautiously. The first step is about safety; later steps test how well the drug works and what the best dose is.

bullets: In a **blind trial** the patients do not know whether they are getting the drug or the placebo.

In a **double-blind trial** **neither the patients nor the doctors** know who has the real drug and who has the placebo until the trial is over. This stops doctors, even unconsciously, treating or judging patients differently, which would cause **bias**.
Patients are allocated to groups **randomly**, so the groups are similar and differences are due to the drug.
A **control group** (placebo) allows fair comparison; the only difference should be whether the drug is given.
A **large number of patients** makes results more reliable and less affected by chance.
core.p: To judge whether the drug itself caused an improvement, researchers compare patients who take the drug with patients who do not. Many people feel better simply because they believe they are being treated; this is the **placebo effect**. A **placebo** is a substance that looks like the real drug but contains no active drug.

bullets: Peer review checks the trial was **fair** (properly controlled, enough patients) and that the **conclusions are supported by the data**.
Publication allows **other scientists to repeat** the investigation; reproducible results are more trustworthy.
It reduces the risk of **bias**, for example a company only reporting results that make its drug look good.
Only after successful trials, review and approval can doctors prescribe the drug, and it is still monitored for side effects.
Link to other topics: evaluating evidence in How Science Works (reliability, validity, bias, ethics).
core.p: When the trial ends, scientists publish their results so others can check them. **Peer review** means that other independent scientists in the same field read the report and judge whether the methods and conclusions are valid before it is published. This helps to prevent false claims and mistakes, and other scientists can repeat the work.

bullets: **Volunteers** can be exposed to risks in early trials, so safety checks and consent are vital.
**Cost**: development takes years and costs enormous sums, which is why drugs are patented and can be expensive for health services.
**Placebo use**: patients in the placebo group may not receive an effective treatment, which is an ethical concern if a treatment already exists.
**Benefit versus risk**: society must weigh the benefit of a new drug against possible side effects.
core.p: Developing drugs involves decisions beyond biology. Exam questions can ask you to discuss both sides. A good answer gives reasons for and against, and avoids simply stating an opinion with no reason. **Animal testing**: protects people and may reduce harm, but animals can suffer and animal results do not always predict the human response.

bullets: **Discover or make** the candidate drug (plants, microorganisms or synthesis by chemists).
**Preclinical testing** on cells, tissues and live animals for toxicity, efficacy and dose.
**Clinical trials** on healthy volunteers (low dose, safety) then on patients (optimum dose, efficacy).
Trials are **double-blind** with a **placebo** and random allocation.
**Peer review** and publication of results; licence for use; continued monitoring.
The order matters: **safety is checked first**, in the lab and then in healthy people, so patients are not exposed to a dangerous drug.
core.p: A very common exam task is to put the stages in the correct order or to explain why each stage is needed. Learn the sequence and the purpose of each step, so you can say what is tested and why that comes first.

exam: **State/Name (1 mark)**: give one precise word, such as 'placebo' or 'foxglove'. Do not add extra text that might contradict it.
**Define (1 to 2 marks)**: use the board wording, for example 'toxicity is how harmful the drug is' and 'efficacy is how well the drug works'.
**Describe the stages (3 to 4 marks)**: use the sequence cells and tissues, live animals, healthy volunteers at low dose, patients to find optimum dose. Each stage with its purpose earns a mark.
**Why use a placebo? (2 marks)**: so that the effect of the drug can be compared with no drug; because patients may feel better just by thinking they are being treated.
**Why double-blind? (2 marks)**: so that neither patients nor doctors are biased, as they do not know who is receiving the real drug.
**Why is peer review important? (2 marks)**: other scientists check the methods and conclusions so results are valid and reliable and bias or errors are reduced.
**Evaluate/discuss (6 marks)**: give arguments for and against (for example animal testing) with reasons, link to evidence and end with a justified conclusion.
**Data questions**: if given a dose table, find the dose with highest benefit and lowest side effects and name it the optimum dose; quote figures from the data.
**Always link** a stage to a reason: 'tested in healthy volunteers at a low dose **to check it is safe**'.
**Command word 'Explain'** needs a because: say why each step is carried out, not only what it is.

mistakes.r: Efficacy is how well the drug works; toxicity is how harmful or safe it is.
mistakes.w: Efficacy means how safe a drug is.

mistakes.r: Double-blind means neither the patients nor the doctors know until the trial is finished.
mistakes.w: Double-blind means the patients do not know which drug they have.

mistakes.r: A placebo contains no active drug; it looks like the drug but has no drug effect.
mistakes.w: A placebo is a weaker dose of the drug.

mistakes.r: Healthy volunteers are given a low dose to test safety; patients are used to find the optimum dose and efficacy.
mistakes.w: Drugs are tested on healthy volunteers to see if they cure the disease.

mistakes.r: Fleming discovered that the Penicillium mould made a substance that killed bacteria; others later developed it into a usable drug.
Most new drugs are synthesised by chemists, although some start from plant chemicals.
mistakes.w: All drugs now come from plants.

mistakes.r: Cells and tissues are tested first; live animals are then used to see the effect on a whole body, including toxicity and dose.
mistakes.w: Animal testing is done to check the drug works in cells.

mistakes.r: Independent scientists in the same field evaluate the work before publication.
mistakes.w: Peer review means the company checks its own results.

summary: You need to describe how new drugs are discovered (from plants and microorganisms, or made by chemists) and how they are developed: preclinical testing on cells, tissues and animals, then clinical trials on volunteers and patients, with placebos, double-blind design and peer review. It matters because it explains why medicines are safe and how scientists judge evidence.

terms.d: A substance that alters the way the body works, used to treat, cure or prevent disease or relieve symptoms.
How harmful a substance is; how poisonous or damaging a drug is to the body.
How well a drug works; whether it produces the intended effect in treating a disease.
The amount of a drug given to a patient.
The dose that gives the best effect with the fewest harmful side effects.
Testing of a new drug in the laboratory on cells, tissues and live animals before it is given to humans.
Testing of a new drug on human volunteers and patients.
A substance that looks like the real drug but contains no active drug, used for comparison.
A trial in which the patients do not know whether they are receiving the real drug or a placebo.
A trial in which neither the patients nor the doctors know who has the real drug or the placebo until the trial is over.
Evaluation of scientific work by other independent scientists in the same field before it is published.
A heart drug extracted from the foxglove plant.
A painkiller developed from salicylic acid, originally found in willow bark.
An antibiotic made by the mould Penicillium, discovered by Alexander Fleming.
An unwanted effect of a drug in addition to its intended effect.
Feeling better because you believe you are being treated, even though no active drug was given.

worked.ans: The drug is first tested on cells and tissues and then on live animals to check it is not toxic and that it works. It is then tested in a clinical trial on healthy volunteers at a very low dose to check it is safe. Finally it is tested on patients to find the optimum dose and to check its efficacy.
worked.q: Describe how a new drug is tested before it can be prescribed. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: preclinical testing on cells and tissues in the laboratory.
Mark 2: then tested on live animals to check toxicity, efficacy and dose.
Mark 3: clinical trials begin with healthy volunteers at a low dose to check safety.
Mark 4: then patients are used to find the optimum dose and see whether the drug works.

worked.ans: The placebo group is a control, so any difference between the groups is due to the drug and not the placebo effect. Because it is double-blind, neither the patients nor the doctors know who has the real drug until the end of the trial, so their expectations cannot bias the results.
worked.q: A double-blind trial uses a placebo. Explain why. (3 marks)
steps: Placebo allows comparison: a group that gets no active drug.
Patients may feel better because they believe they are treated (placebo effect).
Double-blind: doctors and patients do not know who has the drug, which avoids bias.

worked.ans: Plants, for example foxglove, from which digitalis is extracted for the heart, or willow bark, from which aspirin was developed. Microorganisms, for example the mould Penicillium, which makes the antibiotic penicillin.
worked.q: Name two traditional sources of drugs and give an example of each. (4 marks)
steps: Plants: foxglove gives digitalis (heart drug); willow bark gives the chemical for aspirin.
